messages.author: affa918ed63b6275
messages.subject: ..density.. in stat_bin for categorical data
parts:
Hi list members,

I want to know if this behavior is planned.

When I draw the bar of rate of each category for total count,

d<-data.frame(x=gl(2,10)) # the rates are 0.5 for category 1 and 0.5
for category 2
ggplot(d,aes(x,group=1))+stat_bin(aes(y=..density..))

For categorical data, the density of each bar exceed 0.5.
It is because width of the bar is 0.9 by default,
but for categorical data, the width of the bar has no meaning more
than just appearance, unlike for continuous variable.

if I specify the width explicitly, the density is correctly calculated:

ggplot(d,aes(x,group=1))+stat_bin(aes(y=..density..),width=1)

but in this case, there is no space between the bars.

So, for categorical data, should the parameter `width' have no effect
on the calculation?
Here I put the example of modification:

StatBin$calculate<-function(., data, scales, binwidth=NULL,
origin=NULL, breaks=NULL, width=0.9, drop = FALSE, right = TRUE, ...)
{
range <- scales$x$output_set()

if (is.null(breaks) && is.null(binwidth) && !is.integer(data$x) &&
!.$informed) {
message("stat_bin: binwidth defaulted to range/30. Use 'binwidth
= x' to adjust this.")
.$informed <- TRUE
}

w<-if(is.integer(data$x))1 else width # use 1 instead of width in
calculating bins for categorical data
r<-bin(data$x, data$weight, binwidth=binwidth, origin=origin,
breaks=breaks, range=range, width=w, drop = drop, right = right)
r$width<-width # width should control the appearance of the bar.

return(r)
}


thanks,

kohske

That patch would fix the bug, but I'm not sure using a density with
discrete data really makes sense.

Hadley

messages.author: affa918ed63b6275
messages.subject: Re: ..density.. in stat_bin for categorical data
parts:
Hi Hadley

I agree. Probably using a density for categorical data does not make sense.
We should use the number (frequency) of each category instead of the
relative frequency (i.e., density), because a part of information will
be lost by using relative frequency.
But in some case, we use the relative frequency (or percentage of each
category), perhaps for the purpose of simplification...

anyway, thanks a lot.

kohske
